analogy.p: Think of the CPU as a chef. The **control unit** is the chef reading the recipe and shouting instructions: 'chop now, stir next'. The **ALU** is the chef's hands doing the real work such as chopping and measuring. The **registers** are the items in the chef's hands and on the chopping board right now. The **cache** is the shelf next to the cooker holding the ingredients used most often, while **RAM** is the fridge across the room and **secondary storage** is the warehouse. The analogy breaks down because a real CPU repeats the same simple steps billions of times per second and works only in binary, whereas a chef makes judgements and can improvise.

bullets: Know the **full names** and abbreviations: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), Control Unit (CU), cache, registers.
Be able to state **one clear function** of each component and add a second detail to reach 2 marks.
Know the **four special-purpose registers**: Program Counter (PC), Memory Address Register (MAR), Memory Data Register (MDR), Accumulator (ACC).
Explain **why cache is faster** than RAM and **why it is small**.
Link components to the **fetch-decode-execute cycle** (who does what at each stage).
Link to **CPU performance**: more cache means fewer slow trips to RAM.
Expect questions that give a scenario and ask which component does a particular job.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.1 (Systems architecture) asks you to know the **common components inside a CPU and the function of each one**: the **ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit)**, the **CU (Control Unit)**, **cache** and **registers**. You are also expected to know the four special registers used in the Von Neumann model (**PC, MAR, MDR and ACC**). Questions are usually 1 to 4 marks and ask you to *state*, *describe* or *explain* what a component does, so the key skill is giving a precise job for each part rather than a vague word like 'it controls the computer'.

bullets: The CPU only understands **machine code**: instructions and data stored as **binary**.
Instructions and data come from **RAM** (primary storage), not directly from the hard drive or SSD.
The CPU does **not store programs permanently**; it only works on what has been loaded into RAM.
Speed of each part matters: **registers are fastest, then cache, then RAM**.
Modern CPUs have **multiple cores**, and each core has its own ALU, control unit and registers.
The CPU is controlled by a **clock** that sets the pace of the cycle (clock speed in Hz, for example 3.5 GHz).
Everything in this topic is about **what each part does and why it is built that way**.
core.p: The **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** is the 'brain' of a computer. It is a single chip (the processor) whose job is to **fetch instructions from main memory, decode them and execute them**, one after another, billions of times per second. To do this it contains several specialised parts that each have a different role: the **control unit** directs everything, the **ALU** does the calculations and logical comparisons, **registers** hold the tiny pieces of data being worked on right now, and **cache** keeps a fast copy of frequently used instructions and data close by. The parts are connected by internal wiring (buses), and the CPU is connected to RAM by the address, data and control buses.

bullets: **Arithmetic operations**: addition, subtraction, and (in simple models) multiplication and division of binary numbers.
**Logical operations**: AND, OR and NOT on bits, used for decisions and for masking or checking data.
**Comparison**: tests such as equal to, not equal, less than, greater than; the outcome decides whether a program **branches** (for example in an IF statement).
**Binary shifts**: moving all bits left or right, which multiplies or divides a binary number by powers of 2.
Inputs come from **registers**; the result is stored back in a register, normally the **ACC**.
Mark scheme phrase: 'performs **calculations** and **logical decisions/comparisons**'.
Do not say the ALU 'controls' anything: **control is the job of the CU**.
core.p: The **ALU** is the part of the CPU that carries out **arithmetic calculations and logical operations** on binary data. Whenever an instruction says add, subtract, compare or combine bits, the ALU does the actual work. It takes its inputs from registers (commonly one from the **accumulator** and one from memory or another register), performs the operation and puts the result back, usually into the **accumulator**. The ALU is the only part of the CPU that actually *calculates*; the control unit only decides which calculation should happen and when.

bullets: Example: ACC holds 12 and the instruction is ADD 7. The ALU computes 12 + 7 = **19** and the **ACC** now holds 19.
Logical example: 1100 AND 1010 = **1000** (each output bit is 1 only if both input bits are 1).
Logical example: 1100 OR 1010 = **1110** (output bit is 1 if either input bit is 1).
NOT 1100 = **0011** (every bit is flipped).
A **left shift by 1** on 00000110 (6) gives 00001100 (12), so a left shift by one place **doubles** the number.
Branching decisions in loops (WHILE, FOR) depend on **ALU comparisons** every time round.
core.h: How the ALU is used in a program
core.p: Every line of high-level code that involves a calculation or a decision eventually becomes machine-code instructions that use the ALU. For example, `total = total + 5` becomes a load, an add and a store: the ALU carries out the add. An `IF age >= 18` statement becomes a compare instruction, which the ALU performs, and the result decides which instruction is fetched next. This is why the ALU is busy during almost all of the **execute** stage of the cycle.

bullets: Main functions: **fetch** instructions, **decode** them, and **control the execution**.
Sends **control signals** (for example a read or write signal on the control bus) to the ALU, registers, memory and I/O devices.
**Decodes** the instruction by splitting it into the **operation** (what to do) and the **operand** (what to do it to).
Controls the **flow of data** to and from the CPU, memory and peripherals.
Uses the **clock** signal to time each step so that components work in sequence.
**Updates the program counter** so the next instruction is fetched (it increments by 1 or jumps to a new address).
Common error: saying the CU 'does the maths'. That is the **ALU**.
core.p: The **control unit** coordinates and controls everything the CPU does. It **fetches instructions** (by telling memory to send the instruction held at the address in the program counter), **decodes** them to work out what each instruction means, and then sends **control signals** to the other parts so the instruction is executed in the right order and at the right time. It also **manages the flow of data** between the CPU, main memory and input/output devices, and keeps all the parts in step with the **clock**. The control unit does not do any calculations itself.

bullets: Fastest storage in the whole computer, **faster than cache and RAM**.
Very small capacity: each stores one value, typically 32 or 64 bits.
Located **inside the CPU** (on the same chip as the ALU and CU).
**General-purpose registers** hold temporary values for calculations; **special-purpose registers** have a fixed job (PC, MAR, MDR, ACC).
Registers are **volatile** like RAM and cache.
They are used at every stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
Why so few? Registers are built from expensive, high-speed circuitry, and each extra register makes the CPU larger and more costly.
core.p: **Registers** are extremely small, extremely fast storage locations **inside the CPU**. They hold the data, instructions and addresses that the CPU is working on at this exact moment, so that the CPU does not need to wait for slower memory. Each register holds just one word (for example 32 or 64 bits), so the total register space is only a few hundred bytes, but because they are part of the processor itself they have the **fastest access time of any memory**. Registers are **volatile**: when the power is off, their contents are lost.

bullets: **PC**: holds the address of the next instruction; **incremented** after each fetch (or changed by a jump/branch).
**MAR**: holds the **address** where data will be fetched from or stored to; the PC's address is **copied** into it at the start of a fetch.
**MDR**: holds the **actual contents** (data or instruction) moving between memory and the CPU; also called the Memory Buffer Register in some books.
**ACC**: stores the **intermediate and final results** of ALU calculations.
Memory trick: MAR = **A**ddress, MDR = **D**ata.
Registers hold values only **temporarily**; permanent storage is secondary storage.
Fetch order: **PC to MAR, memory to MDR, PC incremented**.
core.p: OCR requires you to know four registers by name and function. The **Program Counter (PC)** stores the **address of the next instruction** to be fetched. The **Memory Address Register (MAR)** holds the **address in memory** that is about to be read from or written to. The **Memory Data Register (MDR)** temporarily holds the **data or instruction that has just been fetched from, or is about to be written to, memory**. The **Accumulator (ACC)** holds the **results of calculations** done by the ALU. Together they let the CPU move values between memory and the ALU in an orderly way.

bullets: Cache is **faster than RAM** because it is built from **SRAM** (static RAM) placed right next to the processor, so data has less distance to travel.
Cache is **smaller than RAM** (typically a few KB to tens of MB) because SRAM is **expensive** and takes up lots of chip space.
It stores **frequently used instructions and data**, such as the instructions inside a loop.
Cache is **volatile**: contents are lost when power is off.
**Cache hit** = data found in cache (fast). **Cache miss** = not found, so it must be fetched from RAM (slower).
Programs often reuse the same data/instructions or use data **near** what they just used, so keeping recent data in cache makes hits likely.
Higher cache capacity means **more data kept close to the CPU**, so fewer slow accesses to RAM.
core.p: **Cache** is a small amount of **very fast memory** that sits between the CPU registers and RAM (it is located on or very close to the CPU chip). It stores **copies of the instructions and data that the CPU uses most often or has used most recently**. When the CPU needs something, it checks the cache first: if it is there (a **cache hit**) it can be read far faster than from RAM; if not (a **cache miss**), it is fetched from RAM and a copy is kept in the cache in case it is needed again. The result is that the CPU spends less time **waiting** for data, so overall performance improves.

bullets: L1 cache: **smallest, fastest**, checked first.
L2 cache: **larger, slower than L1**, checked if L1 misses.
L3 cache: **largest, slowest of the cache levels**, often shared between cores.
Larger cache = **more hits** = fewer trips to RAM = **faster processing** (but with diminishing returns).
Larger cache costs more and uses more space on the chip, so manufacturers balance price and speed.
A cache miss costs time because the CPU has to **wait for RAM**.
Exam wording: 'a larger cache allows **more frequently used instructions/data** to be stored close to the CPU, **reducing the time spent fetching from RAM**'.
core.p: Modern CPUs use several cache levels. **Level 1 (L1)** is the smallest and fastest and is built into each core; **Level 2 (L2)** is bigger and a little slower; **Level 3 (L3)** is the largest and usually shared between cores. You do not need to memorise exact sizes for J277, but you must know that **more cache generally improves performance**, up to a point, and that it costs more. Cache size is one of the three factors OCR links to CPU performance, along with **clock speed** and **number of cores**.

bullets: Order from fastest to slowest: **registers, cache, RAM, secondary storage**.
Order from smallest to largest capacity: registers (bytes), cache (KB to MB), RAM (GB), secondary storage (hundreds of GB to TB).
Cost per byte falls as you go down: **registers most expensive, secondary storage cheapest**.
Registers and cache are inside or on the CPU chip; **RAM is a separate component** connected by buses.
Registers, cache and RAM are all **volatile**; secondary storage is **non-volatile**.
The CPU can only execute from RAM/cache/registers, so programs on the SSD must be **loaded into RAM first**.
Rough scale: a register access takes well under a nanosecond; a RAM access takes tens of nanoseconds; an SSD access takes tens of microseconds or more.
core.h: The memory hierarchy: registers, cache, RAM, storage
core.p: Computer memory is a trade-off between **speed, size and cost**. The fastest memory (registers) is the smallest and most expensive per byte, while the slowest (secondary storage) is the largest and cheapest per byte. The CPU always wants data from the fastest level but can only afford a little of it, so it uses small fast memories to hold copies of the most important data from slower, larger ones. Understanding this order explains **why cache exists** at all.

bullets: Step 1 (fetch): **PC address to MAR**; the instruction is read from memory to the **MDR**.
Step 2: the **PC is incremented** to the next address.
Step 3 (decode): the **CU** interprets the instruction (operation ADD, operand 7).
Step 4 (execute): the **ALU** performs 12 + 7 and the result 19 is stored in the **ACC**.
Where is **cache** used? Both when fetching the instruction and when fetching data.
The **control unit** coordinates every step with control signals timed by the clock.
Any question starting 'describe what happens when...' should use **component names in the right order**.
core.h: How the components work together in one instruction
core.p: Consider the instruction ADD 7 with the accumulator holding 12. The **PC** supplies the address of the instruction, which is copied to the **MAR**. The **control unit** sends a read signal so the instruction travels from RAM (or cache) into the **MDR**. The PC is incremented. The CU **decodes** the instruction as 'add 7'. The **ALU** then adds 7 to the value in the **ACC**, and the new value 19 is written back to the **ACC**. At every step the **registers** hold the values being moved, and **cache** may speed up the fetch if the instruction was recently used.

bullets: **Clock speed** (Hz): number of cycles per second; 3 GHz = 3 billion cycles per second.
**Cores**: each core has its own CU, ALU and registers, so a quad-core can work on four tasks at once.
**Cache size**: more cache = more hits = less waiting for RAM.
Performance depends on **all three together** and on the software being written to use them.
More cores does not always mean twice the speed: some tasks cannot be split up.
Higher clock speeds produce more **heat** and use more power.
This topic leads straight into **CPU performance (cs.0.4)** and **embedded systems (cs.0.5)**.
core.p: CPU performance is often judged by three features: **clock speed**, **number of cores** and **cache size**. A higher clock speed means more fetch-decode-execute cycles per second. More cores mean more instructions can be processed at the same time (if the software supports it). A larger cache means the CPU waits less for data from RAM. Each of these affects the components in this topic: a faster clock makes the CU, ALU and registers work faster; extra cores add extra copies of them; extra cache reduces delays between registers and RAM.

bullets: 1 mark: **name** or state a single function ('ALU performs calculations').
2 marks: function **plus** detail ('performs arithmetic **and** logical operations, such as comparisons').
4 marks: link the components in the **right sequence** (PC, MAR, MDR, CU, ALU, ACC).
Always name the **register** by its full name on first use if the question gives only the abbreviation.
Avoid vague words: 'it runs the computer', 'it stores things', 'it is the brain'.
Cache questions need a **reason**: 'it is faster than RAM because it is closer to / built into the CPU'.
If asked about **performance**, tie the answer to waiting less for RAM or processing more instructions per second.
core.p: Most marks on this topic are won by giving one **specific function** per mark and by using the correct technical word. 'Brain of the computer' earns nothing; 'carries out calculations and logical comparisons' earns the mark. For 'describe' or 'explain' questions, add a reason with 'because' or 'so that'. For comparison questions (cache vs RAM, cache vs register), say *both* sides with a comparative word: 'faster', 'smaller', 'more expensive'.

exam: **Describe the function of the ALU [2 marks]**: 'performs arithmetic calculations (1) and logical operations/comparisons (1)'.
**Describe the function of the CU [2 marks]**: 'fetches and decodes instructions (1) and sends control signals to coordinate the other components (1)'.
**What is a register? [2 marks]**: 'a very small, fast storage location in the CPU (1) that holds data/addresses currently being processed (1)'.

**State the purpose of the PC / MAR / MDR / ACC [1 mark each]**: use the exact wording from the terms list: **address of next instruction**, **address of memory location**, **data fetched or to be written**, **result of a calculation**.

**Explain why cache improves CPU performance [3 to 4 marks]**: stores frequently used instructions/data (1); faster to access than RAM (1); CPU spends less time waiting (1); more instructions executed per second (1).
**Compare cache and RAM**: use comparatives for each point: cache is **faster**, **smaller**, **more expensive per byte**, closer to the CPU.
**Give one effect of increasing cache size [2 marks]**: more data stored close to the CPU (1), fewer fetches from RAM so faster processing (1). Remember the drawback if asked: higher cost.
**Command word 'state'**: just give the fact. **'Describe'**: say what happens in order. **'Explain'**: give the reason using 'because' or 'so'.
For **order-of-events** questions give the sequence PC to MAR, MDR, CU decode, ALU execute, result in ACC; mark schemes accept the right order, not extra detail.
Never use brand-level answers like 'Intel i7'; use **generic component names** from the specification.

mistakes.r: The **ALU** performs arithmetic and logical operations; the **CU** controls and coordinates by decoding instructions and sending control signals.
mistakes.w: The ALU controls the computer / the CU does the calculations.

mistakes.r: Cache is **faster, smaller and more expensive** than RAM and holds **frequently used** data and instructions close to the CPU.
mistakes.w: Cache is just extra RAM / cache is the same as RAM.

mistakes.r: Registers hold **a single value** (data, address or instruction) being used **right now** inside the CPU; programs are held in RAM and secondary storage.
The **MAR holds the address**; the **MDR holds the data/instruction** that was fetched.
mistakes.w: The MAR stores the data being fetched.

mistakes.r: The **PC stores the address of the next instruction** to be fetched.
mistakes.w: The PC stores the current instruction.

mistakes.r: Cache is faster because it is **built from fast SRAM close to or inside the CPU**; it is actually **smaller** than RAM.
mistakes.w: Cache is faster because it is bigger.

mistakes.r: State the actual function: the CPU **fetches, decodes and executes instructions**.
mistakes.w: The CPU is the brain of the computer (and nothing else).

mistakes.r: A bigger cache **can reduce waiting for RAM**, but with **diminishing returns**, and it costs more.
mistakes.w: A bigger cache always makes the computer much faster.

mistakes.r: Cache is **volatile**: it loses its contents when power is off.
mistakes.w: Cache is non-volatile because it keeps frequently used data.

summary: The spec asks you to know what each CPU component does: the ALU (arithmetic and logic), the control unit (decoding and control signals), registers (tiny fast storage for current values, including PC, MAR, MDR and ACC) and cache (fast memory holding frequently used data close to the CPU). It matters because every program is executed by these parts working together, and it is the foundation for questions on the fetch-decode-execute cycle and CPU performance.

terms.d: Central Processing Unit: the component that fetches, decodes and executes instructions.
Arithmetic Logic Unit: the part of the CPU that performs arithmetic calculations and logical operations and comparisons.
Control Unit: the part of the CPU that controls and coordinates the other components, fetching and decoding instructions and sending control signals.
A very small, very fast storage location inside the CPU that holds data, instructions or addresses currently in use.
A small amount of very fast memory on or close to the CPU that stores frequently used instructions and data, so the CPU waits less for RAM.
Register that holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
Register that holds the address of the memory location being read from or written to.
Register that holds the data or instruction that has just been fetched from, or is about to be written to, memory.
Register that stores the results of calculations carried out by the ALU.
When the data or instruction the CPU needs is found in the cache.
When the needed data is not in the cache and must be fetched from RAM.
An electrical signal sent by the control unit to direct other components, for example a memory read signal.
Memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off (registers, cache and RAM).
The number of cycles the CPU carries out per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
An operation such as AND, OR or NOT performed on bits, or a comparison that produces a true/false outcome.
Moving all the bits of a binary number left or right, which multiplies or divides it by powers of 2.

worked.ans: The ALU performs arithmetic calculations and logical operations/comparisons on data held in registers, and returns the result, normally to the accumulator.
worked.q: Describe the role of the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) in a CPU. [2 marks]
steps: The ALU is where calculations happen: it performs arithmetic (add, subtract) on binary data (1 mark).
It also performs logical operations and comparisons such as AND, OR, NOT, equal to, greater than (1 mark).

worked.ans: A larger cache can hold more frequently used instructions and data. The CPU therefore gets more cache hits and has to fetch from the slower RAM less often, so it waits less and executes more instructions per second.
worked.q: A processor has a larger cache than a similar processor. Explain how this could improve its performance. [4 marks]
steps: Cache stores frequently used instructions and data (1).
A larger cache can store more of them close to the CPU (1).
So the CPU finds what it needs in cache more often (more cache hits) instead of fetching from slower RAM (1).
This reduces waiting time, so more instructions can be processed per second (1).

worked.ans: ALU; new ACC value = 00010011 in binary = 19 in denary.
worked.q: The accumulator contains the binary value 00001100 and the instruction ADD 00000111 is executed. State which component performs the addition, and give the new value in the accumulator in binary and denary. [3 marks]
steps: The addition is done by the ALU (1).
Binary check: 19 = 16 + 2 + 1 = 00010011 (1 for correct binary, 1 for correct denary).
